title: Weight-sparse transformers have interpretable circuits
claim: Train a model whose weights are sparse, then prune it per task to a small, readable subgraph of nodes and edges.
layout: Single panel, left-to-right: model stack zooms via dotted lines into a node graph
description: The figure shows the setup in one panel. A text-prompt box reads print("Circuit sparsity") with a stacked, shaded copy of the box, and arrows point to a stacked blue box containing the closing characters "), which is the predicted next token. Below it on the left, a vertical spine feeds three stacked white rounded rectangles, standing in for transformer blocks, with an ellipsis underneath. Dotted lines run from the middle block and widen into a zoomed-in node graph on the right. The graph has three rows of six circles linked by thin arrows. Nearly all nodes and edges are pale grey, meaning they were pruned. A few nodes in shades of blue are joined by thick dark-blue arrows, tracing the surviving circuit. A caption at the bottom right reads "All pruned nodes are mean ablated". The eye goes first to the blue path.
caption: An illustration of our overall setup. We first train weight-sparse models. Then, for each of a curated suite of simple behaviors, we prune the model down to the subset of nodes required to perform the task. We ablate nodes by pruning to their mean activation value over the pretraining distribution.
abstract: Finding human-understandable circuits in language models is a central goal of the field of mechanistic interpretability. We train models to have more understandable circuits by constraining most of their weights to be zeros, so that each neuron only has a few connections. To recover fine-grained circuits underlying each of several hand-crafted tasks, we prune the models to isolate the part responsible for the task. These circuits often contain neurons and residual channels that correspond to natural concepts, with a small number of straightforwardly interpretable connections between them. We study how these models scale and find that making weights sparser trades off capability for interpretability, and scaling model size improves the capability-interpretability frontier. However, scaling sparse models beyond tens of millions of nonzero parameters while preserving interpretability remains a challenge. In addition to training weight-sparse models de novo, we show preliminary results suggesting our method can also be adapted to explain existing dense models. Our work produces circuits that achieve an unprecedented level of human understandability and validates them with considerable rigor.
